activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
story:
Nicolas pressed the knife down on the onion, and nothing happened. The blade sat there like a paperweight. He pushed harder, and it slid sideways off the slick skin and banged against the cutting board, close to his curled fingers.

"Whoa," said Harlyn, from the other side of the kitchen counter. "My money was on the onion winning, but not this fast."

"This knife is useless," Nicolas said. He turned it over, looking for some hidden flaw. "It's not even that old."

Harlyn's grandmother came in from the garden with dirt on her hands, took one look at the board, and swapped his knife for a thinner one from the wooden block. "Try that," she said, and went back outside without another word.

Nicolas set the new blade on the onion, expecting to have to lean on it. He barely pressed at all, and the onion fell open into two clean halves. He tried a slice. Almost no pressure. The knife did the work. He stood there holding the thing like it was magic. So that was the problem. The dull knife had needed him to shove it, and the shoving was what made it slip. The sharp one never had a chance to skate off anything.

"Harlyn, come look at this," he called. "I figured out why I nearly lost a finger." He explained it fast, hands moving: the dull one had to be forced, and forcing was what made it jump. "So a sharp knife is actually the safer one. Less pressure, less slipping."

"That's the weirdest safety tip ever," Harlyn said. "Let's see if it works on the tomatoes."

It did. Nicolas curled his fingertips under, knuckles forward like Ms. Vogel had shown them in cooking club, and the tomato split neatly instead of rocketing across the counter. By the time the onion and garlic were sizzling in the pan, he had the whole rhythm: claw grip, thin slices, oil hissing like applause. The sauce went from pale to deep red, and the smell drifted out the kitchen door toward the garden.

When they ate, Nicolas twirled a forkful of pasta and pointed at Harlyn with it. "Next week I'm teaching you the knife thing."

"You realize you learned it an hour ago," Harlyn said.

"Exactly," said Nicolas. "Still warm."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
story:
Emma had been counting on the cows all week. The nature reserve had a small working dairy farm at its edge, and Ms. Malik had promised the class they could watch the morning milking. On the bus, Emma leaned across the aisle to Johan and Aida and said, "I'm going to figure out how much milk one cow gives. For my science project. If I time it and measure the pipes, I can calculate it."

"Sure," Johan said, though he was already looking out the window at the pines.

The milking barn smelled of warm hay and something sharp and grassy, and the pipes overhead hummed while machines clicked in a steady rhythm. Emma counted the cows in the stalls. Fourteen, all with swollen udders. She pulled out her notebook and started sketching the layout, but a thought snagged her, the way a loose thread catches on a nail. Every cow here had milk. But how? Last summer, at her grandmother's village, Emma remembered a goat named Pepper who had milk only after her twins were born. Before that, Grandmother had said, Pepper gave nothing at all. Emma had been seven and had thought it was strange, then forgotten it.

She looked down the row of stalls again. Beside the far end, past the last milking cow, there was a separate pen, and in it stood a cow with no calf, and her udder was flat. Emma felt her stomach do a small flip. "Johan," she whispered, "look at that one. She's not being milked."

"So? Maybe she's sick."

Emma tested a hypothetical idea out loud, keeping her voice low. "Maybe a cow only makes milk if she's had a calf." Johan shrugged. Aida, who had been listening, frowned and said, "But then every cow in this barn must have had a calf. All fourteen." It sounded like a paradox to Emma, milk everywhere but only because of something absent, something you could not see, the calves who were somewhere else. She revised her whole plan in her head. Timing pipes was useless. She needed to know where the calves were.

She walked to the fence and asked the farmer, a woman in green boots, "Where are the calves?"

"Some in the hutch pens past the barn," the farmer said. "That first-year heifer there hasn't calved yet, so there's no milk from her."

Emma wrote it down with cold fingers: a dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf. The whole hidden rule, sitting right there in her notebook. She turned and waved her pen at Johan and Aida. "Come on. We're going to the hutches."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
The cultural festival had taken over the whole park, with tents for food, dancing, and crafts, but Blake walked past all of it toward the synagogue's booth, where a rehearsal table waited. In two weeks he would read from the Torah scroll for his bar mitzvah, and he had spent a month practicing from a printed book that portrayed the words with vowels and little musical marks above and below the letters. Elisha and Caelan came with him, partly for support and partly because the booth was giving out free honey cake.

Ms. Yilmaz, who ran the booth, set a wooden case on the table and opened it. Inside lay the actual scroll Blake would read from, its parchment a warm cream color, the handwritten letters sharp and black. Blake leaned close, and his stomach dropped. There were no vowels. There were no musical marks at all. "How am I supposed to know the tune from this?" he asked.

"Look again," Caelan said. "Read the letters out loud, slowly."

Blake did. Something strange happened. As he moved along the line, the melody from his practice book rose in his head by itself, attached to the shapes of the words. The printed book had not just shown him the music; it had stitched the tune into his memory of the passage. "The scroll doesn't have the notes," he said slowly, testing the idea, "because I'm supposed to already know them. From the book." He tried a full phrase, chanting it, and it came out right, the rise and fall landing where the marks would have been.

Elisha grabbed his arm. "That's why your practice book exists! It's like a cheat sheet you memorize so the real thing can be blank."

Blake tried another verse and stumbled on one word, then laughed at himself and tried again. Ms. Yilmaz smiled and turned the scroll to his actual portion. "Whenever you're ready."

That night Blake wrote a message to his grandfather, who lived too far away to attend.

Dear Grandpa, you won't believe what happened today. The real scroll has no vowels or musical marks, so everything I learned from my practice book has to live in my head. At first I panicked, but it turns out a month of practicing every night actually worked. I was biased against my own memory, I guess. I thought I needed the marks on the page, explicit and right in front of me, and I didn't. Caelan and Elisha cheered so loud that people at the falafel tent turned around. Two more weeks. I'll call you after.

The morning of the ceremony, Blake stood in front of the open scroll, took a breath, and began to chant.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a quotation inside another quotation uses single quotation marks within the double ones.
story:
Ava sat at the corner table in the school library with her notebook open to a page of squiggles that were supposed to be quotation marks. Her story was due tomorrow, and her climax kept going flat. In her draft, a girl named Marisol races home through a turbulent storm to tell her family that she won the art contest, and Ava wanted Marisol's words to feel like thunder. Instead they sat on the page like wet paper.

"I keep messing up the part where Marisol repeats what her brother said," Ava told Adalyn, who was working two seats away on a poster that was supposed to symbolize courage for a health project. Adalyn leaned over, chewing the end of a grape-scented marker. The line read: Marisol shouted, "Dad, Mateo told me, you draw better than anyone!"

"That looks wrong," Adalyn said. "But I don't know why."

Ava stared at it. She remembered sitting at her grandmother's kitchen table last summer, copying sentences from an old paperback while the fan rattled and the smell of burnt toast drifted from the kitchen. In one of those sentences, a character had said, "She called it 'the long goodbye.'" Ava had copied it twice, backward and forward, without thinking. Now the memory surfaced like a coin glinting at the bottom of a pool. The book had used little marks inside the big ones. She hadn't invented that; she had seen it.

She had a way to test it. Mr. Nielsen's writing shelf held a stack of novels, and Ava pulled one off and flipped until she found a character quoting someone. There it was again: double marks outside, single marks inside. She grabbed a second book, then a third, checking every time someone repeated another person's words. Same pattern every single time. Her insight felt solid enough to stand on, so she went back and rewrote the line: Marisol shouted, "Dad, Mateo told me, 'You draw better than anyone!'"

"That looks right," Adalyn said, tapping the single marks with her marker. "Like smaller doors inside bigger doors."

Ava rewrote her climax so the storm, the shouting, and the single marks inside the double ones all crashed together on the last page, and when she read it aloud under her breath, she could almost hear the rain. She was still grinning when Mr. Nielsen stopped by the table, glanced at her page, and slid a printout in front of her. The contest rules were printed at the top, and under format it said: entries must be handwritten in ink, final drafts only, no computer corrections. Ava looked down at her notebook, at the beautiful corrected line, and then at her left wrist, still in a brace from the skateboard fall that made handwriting hurt.

"First clean copy in the morning," Mr. Nielsen said, and walked away.

Ava picked up her pen with her right hand and wrote one shaky word. "Marisol."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: In 1837, ornithologist John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches.
story:
Brooklyn sat in the waiting room of the vet clinic with her science poster across her knees, and the poster was still blank. Tim had brought in a shoebox with a limp sparrow his cat had caught, and while Ms. Bighorn, the vet, examined the bird behind the counter, Brooklyn had exactly one hour before her mom picked her up. The presentation on natural selection was due tomorrow morning, and the first period bell would not wait.

"You could do moths," Tim offered, peeking over the half door. "Moths that match the trees. Everyone does moths."

"I want to do the finches," Brooklyn said. She flipped through her notebook, where she had sketched three beaks: one thick like a nutcracker, one long and thin, one curved like a tiny parrot's. "Darwin collected birds on the Galápagos Islands, and the beaks are different on different islands. Thick beaks where the seeds are big and hard. Thin beaks where the bugs hide in bark. I just can't figure out how to show it."

Skylar slid into the chair beside her, back from the front desk with a pamphlet about bird feeders. "The problem is you can't see it happening. Nobody watched a beak change."

"That's the part that's bugging me," Brooklyn admitted. She tapped her sketches. "It's like a hidden cause. The beaks don't change on purpose. But why would Darwin's own birds fool him? He was this famous observer, and he didn't even know what he had." Skylar frowned at that, so Brooklyn made a note to check it, because half-remembered facts were worse than none.

"Actually," Skylar said, reading further in the pamphlet's small print, "there's a story in here. In 1837 an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were actually a new group of closely related finches."

"Wait. He thought they were wrens? Blackbirds?" Brooklyn leaned over to see the paragraph herself. "So the birds looked so different that Darwin mislabeled them, and a bird expert had to sort it out. That's almost better than my idea." She felt oddly relieved, too, because last week at the community garden she had called a warbler a sparrow, and Skylar had laughed for a whole bus ride. Even Darwin had gotten birds wrong, and Darwin kept finch skins in jars.

Then she had it. "The feeders," she said, pointing at the wall behind the counter, where the clinic sold tubes of seed and little dishes of nectar. "Ms. Bighorn, can I borrow two kinds of seed? Big striped ones and tiny ones. Just for a demo."

Ms. Bighorn came out with the sparrow cupped in her hands, blinking but alive, and set a scoop of striped sunflower seed and a scoop of millet on the counter. Brooklyn grabbed tweezers from her pencil case and a binder clip from her poster bag. "Tim, you're the thin beak with the tweezers. I'm the thick beak with the clip. Same bowl of mixed seed, thirty seconds. Go."

The tweezers snatched millet grains quickly but could barely crack a striped seed, and the clip crushed the big seeds easily but fumbled the tiny ones. They ran it twice to make sure, and it came out the same both times, which was the logic of the whole thing written in seed hulls. For her poster Brooklyn drew the tools as beaks, arrows from each island's food to each island's bird, and a bold caption to emphasize the point: beaks match the job.

At the bottom she taped her sketch of a small brown bird and wrote, "Counterfeit blackbird. Actually a finch, according to John Gould, 1837. Darwin got fooled too." Skylar laughed when she read it, then took out a pen and drew a tiny speech bubble on the bird that said, "Gotcha."

Ms. Bighorn carried the sparrow past them toward the door, still blinking. "You three want to release him outside? He's ready." Tim grabbed the shoebox, Brooklyn rolled her poster, and Skylar held the door as the bird whirred up into the maple tree and landed, squarely, on the sunflower feeder with the big striped seed.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
The driving school sat in a strip mall between a nail salon and a vacant shop with a faded FOR LEASE sign, and behind the classroom, in a little back room with a sink and a folding table, Ms. Morales kept a washer and dryer. "The landlord lets me have them back here," she told Noah on his first day, "as long as I keep the door shut during lessons." Noah's mother worked late on Tuesdays, so after class he waited forty minutes in that back room, and that was where he was standing when his brother called.

"I need the blue shirt for my interview tomorrow morning," his brother said. "The one I washed last night. It's still in the dryer, I think. Can you fold it and put it on my bed?"

Noah opened the dryer and pulled out the shirt. It was a disaster. Deep creases ran across the chest and the sleeves looked like crumpled paper. He shook it out, he smoothed it flat on the table with both palms, but the creases stayed, set hard into the fabric. He called his brother back. "It's wrecked," he said. "It was in there all night."

His brother groaned, and Noah heard him pacing. "Hang on," Noah said. He was thinking. His brother's other good shirt, the grey one, was in the hamper unwashed, and Noah had never done a load of laundry in his life, but he had watched his mother sort colours, and he had two hours. He dug through the hamper, kept the grey shirt away from a red sock and a muddy towel, measured the detergent the way he remembered, and started the washer. Then he sat on a plastic chair with his permit manual and read about right-of-way until the cycle ended.

Lux, who was waiting for a ride too, wandered in while the dryer was still tumbling. "You have a fertile imagination if you think that grey thing is going to save him," Lux said, pointing at the wrinkled blue shirt still lying on the table. "Maybe," Noah said. When the dryer buzzed, he was standing right beside it. He pulled the grey shirt out while it was still warm and soft, laid it on the folding table, and smoothed it flat. Where the blue shirt had hardened into ridges, the grey one came out smooth and stayed smooth. Noah folded it into a neat square, then a rectangle, and it looked like something from a store shelf.

Ms. Morales came back to lock up and found him still studying the two shirts side by side. "The one I took out right away," Noah said, holding up the grey, "and the one that sat in there overnight." He slid the folded grey shirt into his backpack, careful not to crush it. "Tell my brother I'm on my way," he said to no one in particular, and jogged out to the curb to wait for the headlights.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
story:
Jasmine had agreed to watch the neighbor's baby for exactly ninety minutes, which had sounded manageable until she was actually standing in the park with a stroller, a cooler, and the baby's eight-year-old brother Knox, who had brought a walkie-talkie for no reason she could determine. On the hill beyond the playground, a wind turbine turned its slow white circle, and Knox narrated every rotation like a sports announcer. The baby, Rohan according to the instructions, was supposed to eat at one o'clock, and it was one o'clock.

Jasmine dug through the cooler. Inside was a small jar of oatmeal, a bottle, a plastic bag of crackers, and a squeezable honey bear. A note from the parents was taped inside the lid. She read it while Knox attempted to climb the slide backwards.

The note said: "Feeding plan attached. IMPORTANT: no honey for Rohan until he is 12 months old. Honey can contain bacteria spores that grow in a baby's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism. Yes, even a tiny taste. Yes, even mixed into things." There was a smiley face drawn after this, which Jasmine felt did not match the content at all.

She had been about to stir honey into the oatmeal, on the theory that babies preferred things sweet. She put the honey bear down on the bench like it was a live grenade. "Do your parents leave notes like this a lot?"

"Mom leaves notes on everything," Knox said. "The microwave has a note. It's her whole personality."

Jasmine thought about the spores, invisible things sitting in the honey, waiting. You couldn't see them. The only way to know the rule existed was to read it, and she almost hadn't. She fed Rohan the plain oatmeal instead, and he ate it with enormous enthusiasm, smearing most of it into his own hair.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Yasmina, who babysat for another family on this street and had offered backup advice.

Yasmina: "how's it going? btw if Knox tries the red berries by the fountain, those are toxic. also did you check the parents' note? the LAST sitter gave that baby honey. she felt so bad she cried at the block party."

Jasmine typed back: "I checked it. Nobody is germinating anything in anybody's gut on my watch." She was pleased with that sentence. She was less pleased a minute later, when she turned around and found Knox had taken off his shoe and was attempting to plant a dandelion seed in it, explaining that it would germinate by Friday. The walkie-talkie crackled with static from his pocket.

The parents arrived at 2:40. The mother inspected Rohan, found one shoe, one cracker, and a large quantity of oatmeal in his hair, and declared the afternoon a success. Then she sat down on the bench, unscrewed the honey bear, and squeezed a long golden ribbon into her own thermos of tea.

"More for me, then," she said.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
Gabriel curled his fingers into what the video had called the claw grip, knuckles forward like a tiny armor, and lowered the knife toward the onion. Daniela leaned on the counter beside him, watching with the patience of someone who had already been told twice not to touch the blade. "Slower," she said. "The onion isn't going anywhere." Gabriel moved the edge down and felt it bite through the layers, and his eyes began to sting so badly he had to resign himself to chopping half-blind, trusting the claw to keep his fingertips out of the blade's path. A tear slid down his cheek anyway. "How does it even know?" he muttered. "It's a vegetable."

The sauce was Mr. Romano's idea, sort of. He had come over to fix the porch light, smelled garlic from the kitchen, and poked his head in. "From scratch?" he'd said. "Good. Restaurant sauce is just ketchup wearing a suit." Gabriel had decided to take that as a compliment to his ambitions. Now he had a pan of crushed tomatoes bubbling, and the pasta was boiling in the big pot, and the whole kitchen smelled like something sophisticated that he had made himself.

The sauce looked thin, though. Watery at the edges. Gabriel tipped the pot toward the sink to dump the pasta water, all of it, the cloudy frothing mess swirling against the lid.

"Wait." Daniela grabbed his wrist. "Save a cup of that." Gabriel stared at her. "The gray water? It looks like dishwater." "It's not just water," she said. "Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta." He squinted at the cloudy surface. So the fog in the pot was the hidden thing, the reason the water looked wrong, and maybe the reason his sauce looked wrong too.

He ladled out a cup, dumped the rest, and added the splash slowly, stirring. He watched. The sauce turned glossy where the water went in, then seemed to tighten around the spoon. He added a little more, testing, and the bubbles changed from flat and sloppy to slow and round. "It's clinging," he said. "Look at it. It's actually clinging."

They took their bowls to the porch steps and ate while the sky went orange. Mr. Romano, packing up his toolbox, paused on his way to the truck and leaned over for a look. "Sauce from scratch, onions chopped by a boy who still has ten fingers," he observed. "Consensus around here is you'll do it again next week?" "I'll do it again Friday," Gabriel said, and twirled his fork.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
The track ringed the hockey rink on a suspended walkway, four laps to the eight hundred metres, and Brielle had gone out too fast in every race so far. In her last attempt she led the first lap and then watched the rest of the field come past her one by one, as though her legs had simply evaporated somewhere on the back straight. Today she wanted to fix that, and Robert and Chase were racing the same distance in the next heat, so she asked them to shout out lap times for her.

She stood at the line with the problem turning over in her mind. Her instinct was to sprint the start, because leading felt like winning, even when it was not. But feeling fast and being fast were two different things, and how a race felt in the first lap was subjective and useless for judging what she could do in the second. She decided on a simple test. She would hold back on purpose, take the first lap at what felt like almost nothing, and see what she had left.

The starter called them up. Brielle let three runners go past her in the first fifty metres, and it took effort to keep her arms loose and her stride short when her whole body wanted to chase. "Forty-one," Robert called from the rail as she crossed the line for lap one. She did not know yet whether that was good. She only knew she was not tired.

On the second lap she passed one runner, then another. Her legs still answered when she asked for more, and she took the final bend hard and crossed the line second in her heat. She bent over the rail, breathing hard but not empty. Chase was leaning next to her, already finished from the earlier heat. "What was your last lap?" he asked. "Thirty-seven," she said. He held up his own times. His first lap had been thirty-six and his last one thirty-nine. He had gone out fast and slowed down, the opposite of what she had done.

"You know there's a name for that," Robert said, climbing over the rail with the stopwatch. "Second half faster than the first is called a negative split. First half faster is called a positive split." He showed her the two sets of numbers side by side, his finger moving between the laps.

Brielle looked at the times again and felt something settle. She had run a negative split and finished second. Chase had run a positive split and won his heat. "So which one is actually better?" she asked. Robert shrugged and Chase grinned, still holding his times up where she could see them.

"Do it again next week," Chase said, "and bring a stopwatch."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
Piper had been training for the track team tryouts since September, which meant three weeks of jogging around the block and one afternoon of actual sprinting, and now she stood at the white line of the school track wondering which of those had prepared her.

"Lane four," said Mr. Campbell-Brown, holding a clipboard like it owed him money. "Two laps, then we time the sprints."

Zander was in lane three, stretching in a way that suggested he had read about stretching. Emiliano was in lane five, bouncing on his toes. Then the whistle went, and thinking stopped mattering.

By the second lap Piper had found a rhythm, until the runner in lane two, a boy she only knew as the one who wore the same green hoodie every day, clipped the inside curb and went down hard. His head bounced off the rubberized track with a sound Piper would have preferred not to hear. He stood up almost immediately, swaying like a fence in wind, and waved at Mr. Campbell-Brown. "I'm fine. I can finish. This is my only shot at the team."

Mr. Campbell-Brown was already walking toward him, and the tryouts paused while everyone tried to look like they weren't watching. Piper drifted closer, catching the edge of the conversation.

"You sit out," Mr. Campbell-Brown said. "It's not my choice. It's the Zackery Lystedt Law. Washington passed it in 2009, and it was the first state law in the country that says a young athlete with a suspected concussion comes out of play and stays out until a health professional clears them."

"Then I'll just say I don't have a concussion," the boy said.

"That's not how being cleared works, and you know it."

Piper watched him process this. He argued about delaying it, then about postponing it, then about running one slow lap as a compromise, which was like negotiating with weather. Mr. Campbell-Brown wrote something on his clipboard and did not look up. Eventually the boy sat on the bench with the reckless expression of someone planning to stand up the moment no one was watching, which, Piper noted, everyone was.

She had assumed he was just being stubborn. But she thought about it while shaking out her legs for the sprints. He didn't want to miss his chance, and he figured one more lap couldn't hurt. That was the hidden math: he was treating the risk like erosion, so small and gradual you could ignore it, when the whole point of the law was that heads don't work that way. She tested the idea on herself. If she fell, would she want to keep running? Yes. Would the rule apply anyway? Also yes. The rule didn't care what you wanted, which was exactly why it existed.

The sprints started. Piper ran her best time of the afternoon, mostly because she was annoyed, and annoyed Piper was fast Piper. When she finished, she walked over to the bench and sat down next to the green hoodie.

"I told Coach my mom can take me to the clinic tonight," he said. "If I'm cleared, I can try out again Thursday."

"That's not so bad."

"It's terrible."

"It's one day later," Piper said, and handed him her water bottle, since his was still lying in lane two.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
story:
The lights went out at seven twenty, right in the middle of Lucas's homework, and the fridge in the kitchen of Grandmother's apartment sighed into silence. Grandmother was in the bedroom resting, and Lucas had been trying to reach his dad, who had promised to call about whether he would visit this weekend. The cordless phone sat in its cradle on the counter, its little screen blank, dead as a stone. When Lucas pressed the buttons, nothing happened at all.

He stood in the dark kitchen holding the useless handset, thinking. The phone had worked this morning, so it was not broken. The power cut had done something to it, which meant the phone needed electricity from the apartment, like a lamp or the toaster. That idea felt strange, because phones were supposed to be their own thing, but it fit what he was seeing. He tried his cell phone next and got one bar, then none, and the call to his dad failed before it rang. Down the hall, Grandmother coughed and asked whether he was all right, and he said yes, though he wasn't, not entirely.

Then he remembered the phone hanging on the kitchen wall, the old one with the curly cord and the push buttons worn smooth. Grandmother called it her stubborn old thing and never used it. It had no screen and no cradle, just a cord that ran into the wall, and Lucas thought that if the cordless one needed the apartment's electricity, maybe this one did not. Maybe the power came from somewhere else, through the line itself. It was a guess, and he could test it the only way there was. He lifted the receiver and put it to his ear.

There was a dial tone. Lucas laughed out loud in the dark kitchen, a startled, delighted sound. He dialed his dad's number by feel, pressing each worn button, and after two rings his dad answered, his voice small and crackly through the old speaker. They talked for six minutes about the weekend, and his dad said Thursday was better, and Lucas said that worked, and neither of them said what they were both thinking, which was that Thursday was not the same as Saturday. When the call ended, the dial tone hummed in his ear like a small steady heartbeat.

Grandmother came out in her robe, feeling her way along the wall, and Lucas let her listen to the dial tone. She pressed the receiver to her ear and went quiet. "That's the phone your grandfather installed," she said finally. "I keep meaning to take it down." She hung it back on its hook without taking it down, her fingers lingering on the intricate braid of the cord. Lucas found the flashlight in the drawer to illustrate where the candles were, because the dark was going to last a while yet, and Grandmother's chest had been raspy for days, the start of some infection the doctor was treating with pills. He lit the candles one by one. From the wall, faintly, the phone chirped, and Grandmother reached for it.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
story:
The poster showed Marcus Delgado, sixth-grade candidate for student council president, sitting in the cafeteria with a tray of nachos, laughing with kids at a long table. Nicholas stopped in the hallway and stared at it. Marcus looked like the most ordinary boy in the world, like somebody who ate nachos every day and shared his fries. Nicholas had never once seen Marcus eat in the cafeteria; he always went home for lunch. Below the photo, in fat green letters, it said, "One of us. One of us. VOTE DELGADO."

"You're blocking the water fountain," said Olive, tapping his shoulder.

"Look at this poster," Nicholas said. "He's never in that cafeteria. I've got lunch fourth period. He's out of here by the time the bell rings."

Olive shrugged. "It's a good picture, though. Everybody's talking about him. Half the school already has his buttons."

Nicholas walked to class turning that over. Marcus had other posters too. One said, "Ten out of ten seventh graders choose Delgado," which was a number Nicholas doubted, since his own class had voted nothing. Another showed a photo of a local TV weatherman giving a thumbs-up next to the words, "Even he says Delgado brings the sunshine." And one poster called Marcus's opponent, Forrest Chen, a "sneaky schemer" in dripping red letters, while calling Marcus "honest, brave, true." Those words weren't reasons. They were just... loaded, like dice someone had weighted.

At lunch, Forrest sat down across from him with a folded paper. "I made a poster," Forrest said, laying it flat on the table. It showed Forrest at a workbench, holding a hammer. "I take woodshop. It's real. I really do this."

Nicholas tilted his head. "It's good, but it's the same trick. The plain-folks technique, Ms. Njoroge called it once. You show yourself doing an everyday thing so people trust you as one of us." He tapped the photo of Marcus with the nachos. "He's doing it to us right now."

"So what do I do? I can't just write my plan on a poster. Nobody stops to read."

Nicholas thought about the hallway, how everyone slowed down at the fountain, how the walls there ran perpendicular to the gym and made a wide corner everybody had to pass. "You don't put the plan on the poster. You put it in people's hands." He borrowed a marker from a sixth grader and drew a quick sketch on the back of Forrest's paper: a small flyer, the size of a hand, with one question printed large. "It says, what's his actual plan? Then yours on the back."

"Marcus has a plan," Olive said, sitting down with her tray. "He told the assembly he'd get better vending machines."

"He also told the assembly he'd get us a swimming pool," Nicholas said. "We don't have room for a swimming pool. The marching band practices on the only grass we have." He didn't want to intimidate anyone with a big argument. He wanted one small true question, easy to carry, easy to ask out loud.

On Friday, Forrest handed out two hundred flyers by the fountain. Nicholas watched kids read them, watched them look up at Marcus's nacho poster, watched the two things collide quietly in their heads. Some kids asked Marcus's friends, "So what's the actual plan?" and the friends said, "He's one of us," which was an answer to a different question.

When the votes were counted Monday afternoon, Ms. Njoroge read the results over the announcements: Forrest Chen, president, by nineteen votes. Marcus passed Nicholas in the hall later, still wearing his own button, and pulled off the tray of nachos from his newest poster with a shrug.

"Fair enough," Marcus said, and held out the nachos. "Want some? They're from the actual cafeteria. Honest, brave, true."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
story:
The morning they landed at the beach, Luca felt perfect. Ten hours on a plane, a whole ocean behind them, and he had slept fine and eaten the weird airplane noodles and even helped carry his little sister's bag. "Jet lag," his dad had warned before they left, "it'll get you." But it never did. On the second day Luca and Mira, the girl from the rental house next door, dug a moat around a lopsided sandcastle and gave it a guard made from a stick wearing a shell hat. "He's a peasant," Mira decided, patting the stick into the wet sand. "He guards the castle but nobody ever thanks him." Luca added a second stick beside him, defiant against the incoming tide, and they laughed when the water flattened both guards and the peasant's shell hat floated away.

The trip went too fast. Luca postponed packing until the last night because, he told himself, a packed suitcase meant the trip was really ending. When the taxi came, Mira ran down the sand barefoot to hand him the shell hat. "For the peasant's replacement," she said, and her ears went pink.

They flew home the next day, east, back over the same ocean. And this time Luca felt wrecked. At the beach he had bounced out of bed at dawn; now, home, he lay staring at the ceiling at two in the morning, wide awake, then couldn't drag himself up when morning actually came. His stomach grumbled at the wrong hours. He was grumpy at breakfast, sleepy at lunch, alert at midnight. "What's wrong with me?" he complained to his mom. "It was the same length flight both ways."

That was the part that bugged him. Same plane, same hours, same ocean, but only one direction had flattened him. He got a pencil and drew two arrows across a sketch of the world in his notebook, one pointing left to the beach and one pointing right to home, and stared at them until his eyes hurt. On the fourth sleepless night he found Mira online and told her his theory. "Going out, we flew west. Coming home, east. Same distance. So it can't be the flying itself."

Mira sent back a link from her own search, then a single line: "It says most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west." Luca read it twice, then checked a second site, then a third. All the same. It wasn't the plane, or the hours, or the noodles. It was the direction, and somehow he'd been lucky on the way out.

He took the shell hat out of his backpack and set it on his windowsill, ragged edge facing east. Somewhere behind the rooftops, past the whole dark ocean, the tide would be crawling up the ruined castle. "Guard it," Luca told the shell, and turned off his lamp.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
The rumor reached David on Tuesday, in the locker room before practice, when a teammate said Riverside's best runner had been declared ineligible for Saturday's meet. "My cousin heard it from somebody who goes there," the teammate said. "They're going to have to forfeit." David wanted it to be true so badly he could taste it. Riverside had beaten his school three years in a row, and the thought of them losing without a race even being run made him grin all through warm-ups. He told Aiyana about it at lunch, and he told Hailee, and by Wednesday half the eighth grade was repeating it as fact.

Aiyana was the one who frowned. "Who actually checked?" she asked. "Not who heard it. Who checked?" David shrugged, but the question stuck to him like burrs on a sock. He realized he had passed the story along without asking a single question, which was, he had to admit, a little reckless. He also realized something stranger: when Hailee had said the rumor might be wrong, he had felt annoyed, as if she were taking Riverside's side. That feeling seemed worth investigating.

On Thursday he found the Riverside roster online, and there was the runner's name, still listed, with a time from a meet held the previous Saturday. Then he found the league rules, which said eligibility was reviewed before the season, not during it. The roster and the rumor couldn't both be true. One of them was a flat contradiction, and only one of them came from a person he could message. He sent a note to the Riverside student council page, feeling a bit foolish, and by that evening a reply came back: the runner was fine, the rumor had started as a joke in a group chat.

"You know there's a name for what you did," Aiyana said on Friday, when he told her. "Confirmation bias. You believed it because it fit what you already wanted." David winced, but she said it without smugness, just handing him the word the way you hand someone a bandage.

The hard part came after. At practice he had to stand in front of teammates and say the story wasn't true, and a couple of them looked at him like he'd ruined something. One boy muttered that it might still be true, that Riverside was probably hiding it, and David recognized that exact feeling, the one that wants the good news so much it refuses the bad.

Saturday came, and Riverside won again, their runner crossing the line four seconds ahead of David. He stood at the fence afterward, breathing hard, watching the other team celebrate. Aiyana handed him his water bottle. "Next rumor," she said, "we check first." He nodded, still watching the runner, who was doing a victory lap he had absolutely earned.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Ava stood in the food court of the mall, phone hot in her hand, staring at a photo she had posted two days ago: her and Romain goofing around in front of the fountain, with the caption about her audition for the jazz ensemble. Her account was private. She had checked the setting twice. Yet the photo was here, on a stranger's page, reposted with a caption that said, "Found this kid who thinks she can play trumpet."

"Okay, breathe," said Ahmad, sliding into the seat across from her with a tray of nachos. "Tell me the whole thing, from the start. Don't jump around."

Ava forced herself to slow down. She described accepting a follower request a month ago from someone with the username lkelly_04, someone she vaguely remembered from a summer recreation program. Then the audition, then the post, then this. Ahmad tilted his head. "So your page is private, but they follow you."

"That's it," Ava said, and the pieces began to fit together like the sections of a symmetrical origami shape she'd folded in art class: two halves she had thought matched, but one side had a fold she'd missed. "Private means people who don't follow me can't see it. But anyone I already accepted can see everything, and they can take a screenshot and post it wherever they want. It's like the greenhouse Ms. Tesfaye showed us when we studied agriculture. The walls keep most things out, but anything already inside can carry seeds back out."

Ahmad wiped cheese off his fingers. "So lkelly_04 saw it and forwarded it."

"Only one way to test that," Ava said. She posted a new photo, a boring shot of her sneakers, and waited. Ninety minutes later, it appeared on the stranger's page too, same angle, same gray laces. "Confirmed," she whispered. She unfollowed and removed lkelly_04, reported the page, and asked Romain to do the same with any follower he barely knew.

Then came the part that actually helped. Ava messaged the stranger directly: "This is my photo, posted from a private account, and I did not agree to share it." The stranger's page vanished within an hour. When she told Ms. Tesfaye about it at the music room the next afternoon, Ms. Tesfaye nodded slowly and said, "You decomposed the problem instead of panicking. That's exactly how I want you to approach a difficult passage in your audition piece, too."

At the audition on Saturday, Ava lifted her trumpet, the metal cool against her lips. In the third row of chairs, Romain gave her a thumbs up, and beside him Ahmad held up his phone with a note on the screen that read: Playing for us, not for strangers. Ava smiled, took a breath, and began.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause.
story:
Jordan blew his nose, dropped the tissue in the trash can by the couch, and counted. That was the ninth one since breakfast. Tomorrow was Elisha's birthday party, the one with the pizza and the rooftop terrace, and he was not going to miss it over a runny nose. The problem was his mother, who stood in the doorway with a thermometer like a guard holding a key.

"I'm fine," he said. "It's basically gone."

"You were shivering last night." She checked the thermometer again even though she'd already read it. "You have the constitution of a wet paper towel in this family. Every cold finds you."

"It's not every cold. It's one cold."

She went back to the kitchen, and Jordan picked up his phone. He texted Leanna, because Leanna had been sick two weeks ago, right before he was, and they'd shared a booth at the pizza place the day she came back. If they'd had the same thing, then why was he sick now and she wasn't again? He typed, "what were your symptoms," and waited, sniffling, until the three dots appeared.

"Sore throat, fever, couldn't swallow," she wrote. "Why?"

His throat was fine. His was all nose and cough. Weird. He opened the laptop on the coffee table and searched why no cold vaccine. The first result made him sit up. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. Not two, not ten. More than two hundred. And the most frequent cause was something called rhinoviruses. He said the word out loud to the empty living room. "Rhinoviruses."

He called Leanna. "You gave me your cold," he said when she picked up.

"I got better two weeks ago. You can't catch it from me now."

"That's what I mean. We probably didn't even have the same one." He walked to the window with the phone wedged against his shoulder, watching the street. "There's more than 200 different viruses that cause colds. Rhinoviruses are the most common. Your sore throat thing could be one virus and my nose thing could be a different one entirely. That's why there's no single shot for it. You'd need like two hundred shots."

"So you're saying it's not my fault?"

"I'm saying I can't prove it's your fault."

"That's the most romantic thing you've ever told me."

He laughed, then coughed, then laughed again. Here was the part that mattered. He grabbed a notebook from his backpack and wrote a plan: fluids, rest, no staying up, extra vitamin whatever was in the kitchen. He incorporated a walk around the block at four o'clock, because he'd read that light movement helped and he needed to prove to his mother he could function. The fever reading was crucial; if it was gone by morning and he kept the plan tonight, he had a case.

At dinner he set the notebook next to his plate. His mother read it, chewing slowly.

"A walk?" she said. "Tonight?"

"Thirty minutes. Then straight to bed."

She looked at the thermometer on the counter, then at him. "If you have no fever at seven a.m.," she said, "we'll talk about the party."

Jordan was already writing seven a.m. at the bottom of the page.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
story:
Vincent had read the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms twice on the bus to city hall, and both times the words had slid off him like water off a raincoat. Ms. Park's assignment was on the notice board by the council chamber doors: each student had to read one right listed in the constitution and explain it in their own words, out loud, in front of everyone at the mock council session. Vincent's turn was in forty minutes, and he still had nothing.

He found Amina on the bench outside the chamber, holding her own crumpled printout. "What did you pick?" he asked.

"Mobility rights. Easy. You can live and work anywhere in Canada." She glanced at his page. "Which one's yours?"

"That's the problem. Mine says everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person. But when I try to say it in my own words, I just say the same words in a different order."

Amina laughed, then leaned closer. "Okay, here's a thing. My cousins live in Germany, and last summer my uncle showed me their constitution. It's called the Basic Law, from 1949, and Article 1, the very first article, starts with 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.' That's it. That's the first sentence of the whole thing. Before free speech, before anything."

Vincent stared at her. "Dignity comes first? Not rules, not government. Dignity."

"That's what he said. Canada's opens by saying what it is, like a definition. Germany's opens by saying what nobody is allowed to touch."

He tested the idea right there, the way he tested everything, out loud and sideways. "So if dignity is first, then everything after it has to fit underneath it. Even the stuff about who gets to delegate power to whom. Even a section about leisure." He frowned. "Wait, is there a section about leisure?"

"Mobility," Amina said. "You're spiralling."

"Spiritually." But something had clicked. He borrowed her pen, crossed out his notes, and wrote a single sentence at the bottom of the page.

When Ms. Park called his name in the chamber, with the coach from the community league and a bored city clerk watching from the back row, Vincent stood up and read the right word for word first, because that was the rule. Then he closed the paper.

"In my own words," he said. "Your dignity is off the table. It doesn't matter what you did, or what anyone thinks of you. It can't be violated, and it can't be traded away. It's like the floor everything else stands on." He paused. "Some countries say that on line one."

Ms. Park wrote something on her clipboard. "Where did you find that comparison?"

"Amina's cousins," Vincent said. "She shared."

Amina, three rows back, lifted her mobility rights paper and waved it like a flag.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
story:
The pool deck smelled like chlorine and nerves. Felix stood with eleven other kids at 7:40 in the morning, waiting for the coach to post the tryout order for the school swim team, and his stomach was doing slow flips.

"I'm not warming up," Dean said beside him. "I want to watch the first heat instead, see how fast the other guys actually are. Know what we're up against." Felix had planned to do the same thing, sit on the bench and study the competition. But something nagged at his conscience, a memory of last season's time trials, when he had climbed in cold and felt like his arms were made of rope for the first lap. The coach had told nobody anything. He'd just noticed that the kids who jogged the deck loop and did arm swings before racing always seemed to hit their pace in the first lap, not the third. Felix had a theory about that, something he could not see but could test: maybe it was heart rate and muscle temperature, that getting both up somehow made the muscles work better before a hard effort. That was the whole idea, and it was simple enough to try.

"You go watch," Felix said. "I'm going to jog and stretch first." Dean rolled his eyes and headed for the bench. Felix jogged two easy loops of the deck, then did moving stretches, arm circles and leg swings, until he could feel his pulse ticking quicker under his jaw and warmth spreading through his shoulders.

When his heat was called, he climbed onto the block feeling loose, almost buoyant, and when the whistle blew his arms caught the water on the very first stroke. He touched the wall and looked at the board, and there it was: a personal best, in the first race of the morning. Dean swam two heats later, and Felix watched him go out stiff, grinding through the opening lap while the field pulled away. Afterward Dean dragged himself out, breathing hard, shaking his arms out one at a time.

"That water was freezing," Dean said. "It's like my muscles wouldn't turn on."

"Ask Felix," Kianna said from the next lane, wringing out her cap. "He told me he jogged and stretched before his heat. Something about heart rate and muscle temperature."

Dean squinted at him. "So you're saying I swam slow because I skipped it? Paraphrase that for me in one sentence, because it sounds like you're saying I lost to a bench."

"I'm saying the bench beat you," Felix said, and pointed at the team list going up on the wall, where Dean's name sat one spot below the cut line.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the Rhineland, the region of western Germany along the Rhine River next to France, so it could act as a buffer zone.
story:
Chloe spread her history notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled like lemon polish and, faintly, like the mushrooms Grandpa was frying for lunch. "The Treaty of Versailles," she read out loud, "and how it helped lead to the Second World War." She glared at the sentence as if it might apologize and turn into something easier.

"Still stuck on that?" said Isabelle, who had come over supposedly to help, but who was currently balancing a spoon on her nose.

"Mr. Pham wants us to explain why, not just list dates," Chloe said. "And I don't get it. The treaty was in 1919, the war started twenty years later. How does one thing cause the other?"

Grandpa wandered in with a plate of fried mushrooms and a squint at the map she had propped against the sugar bowl. Chloe traced the western edge of Germany with her finger. Then she noticed something odd. A whole stretch of Germany's own land, right along the Rhine River next to France, was shaded on the map's legend as demilitarized. No German troops allowed there. That made no sense to her. It was like drawing a line through your own bedroom and saying nobody from your family could stand in it.

"Grandpa, why couldn't Germany put soldiers in its own land?"

He shrugged happily, because shrugging was one of his favorite activities. "You have a book there. Books know more than grandpas."

So she tested her idea. France had been invaded before and was afraid of it happening again, she thought. If a country wanted to invade France, it would have to march through that stretch along the river. Without troops there, that stretch became something like a wall. She flipped through the treaty book until she found the name: the Rhineland. It wasn't a wall of stone, it was a buffer zone, land left empty of soldiers on purpose.

"It's like the hedge!" Isabelle said suddenly, spoon finally falling off her nose.

"What hedge?"

"The one outside. Come on." Isabelle dragged her out the back door to the garden, where an invasive vine had been sneaking into the yard all summer. Between the vine and the roses stood Grandpa's thick hedge. "The vine wants to invade the roses, but the hedge is in the way. It's a buffer."

Chloe looked at the hedge, then at the vine snaking along the fence, then back at the house. Somewhere behind the kitchen window, fungus was probably already growing on Grandpa's forgotten half of a lemon. Things spread when nothing stops them. Then she ran inside and found the next part in the book herself: Germany later sent troops into the Rhineland anyway, and nobody stopped that either. The wall had been on paper only.

"Here's my whole explanation," she announced, standing on a kitchen chair because it felt more convincing. "France was scared of being invaded, so the treaty made the Rhineland, that strip of Germany along the Rhine next to France, a place with no German troops, a buffer zone. Then Germany broke that rule, and breaking it was like a test nobody stopped. So a man in a kitchen in 1936 looks at the map and sees he can go anywhere."

"That was the spoon's idea, actually," Isabelle said. "I want footnote credit."

"Fine. Footnote: the spoon."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A first thesis is often called a working thesis because it can change; if the evidence points somewhere else, a careful writer revises the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence.
story:
Lucy sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with six library books fanned around her like a card trick gone wrong. Her essay assignment was due Monday: take a position, outline three supporting points, then draft. She had already written her thesis on an index card in purple marker: "Pigeons are a menace to cities and should be driven out." She tapped the card against her chin. Easy. Everyone hated pigeons. Three points would practically write themselves.

By page forty of the first book, she was frowning. The book claimed pigeons were astonishingly smart, could recognize human faces, and had once saved entire flocks of carrier messages during wars. The second book said cities would have a bizarre amount of dropped food litter without pigeons cleaning it up. "Traitors," Lucy told the books. "All of you."

She called Veronica, who showed up ten minutes later with popcorn and zero sympathy. "So your evidence says the opposite of your thesis," Veronica said, munching. "Bummer."

"I can't start over. I have the whole outline. Point one: droppings. Point two: crowds. Point three: they're basically rats with wings." Lucy held up the index card like a shield.

Veronica leaned over the third book. "It says here some pigeons went nearly to extinction because people hunted them. Passenger pigeons. Billions of them, gone." She looked up. "That's sad, not menacing."

Lucy stared at the card. Then she flipped it over, and on the blank side wrote in smaller, less confident purple: "Pigeons deserve a place in cities because they clean up litter, are highly intelligent, and have helped humans for centuries." She frowned at it. "But what do I even call this thing now, since my first one was wrong?"

"Working thesis," said Mr. Suryanto from the doorway, holding a plate of his wife's samosas because he firmly believed studying required snacks. He set it down between them. "That's what my professor called the first one, anyway. It works until the evidence points somewhere else." He shrugged and went back to his own kitchen.

Lucy and Veronica looked at each other. "So the first one wasn't wasted," Lucy said slowly, "it was just... working." She grabbed a fresh index card and started building her new outline. Point one: litter cleanup. She had three sources for that already.

"Menace to cities," Veronica read over her shoulder, laughing. "You really committed to that one."

"I had a whole paragraph planned about a pigeon that stole my sandwich in the plaza." Lucy snatched a samosa. "Fine. New plan. The pigeon keeps the sandwich, and I integrate it into point two as proof of their intelligence." She wrote the sentence down, underlined it twice, and propped the card where she could see it.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Japan, tipping in restaurants is generally not expected, and leaving extra money on the table can confuse the staff.
story:
At the Japanese booth at the cultural festival, Ellie stood in front of a menu written in both English and Japanese, holding a crumpled practice sheet in her pocket. Maika had promised to teach her enough Japanese to order lunch, since Ellie's family was visiting Tokyo in the spring and she wanted to surprise her grandmother by ordering on her own. The plan was simple: three phrases, one order, one question about the price. Ivana had already ordered a plate of yakisoba by pointing at the menu, which felt like cheating to Ellie, though Ivana said it was efficient.

The booth had been set up like a tiny restaurant, with paper lanterns strung along the front and a man in an apron taking orders behind a counter. Maika leaned close and whispered the first phrase, and Ellie repeated it, then wrote it out phonetically on her sheet. When she tried the second one, the word for "how much," she kept slipping into the rhythm of English, and Maika laughed so hard the paper lanterns above them swayed.

"You have to let the sounds land soft," Maika said. "Like dropping a pebble in water, not throwing it."

Ellie tried again, slower this time. The man behind the counter looked up and nodded, so she stepped forward, heart tapping, and said the whole order in one careful line. The words came out smaller than she had practiced, but they came out. Then she asked the price question, and he answered with a number she almost missed. She counted out the bills exactly, added a little extra, and left the coins on the counter beside her tray, the way her family always did at restaurants back home.

She had taken three steps toward the tables when the man came around the counter and caught up with her. He held out the coins in his open palm and shook his head, polite but firm, as if she had dropped her keys. Ellie stared at the shiny coins, and a principle assembled itself in her mind: what looked like politeness at home looked like a mistake here. She remembered a travel show where a server ran a whole block to return change a family had left on the table, and suddenly that scene made sense. Tipping was not part of it at all.

"Keep it," she started to say, then stopped, because Maika was already translating something the man said, quick and gentle.

"He says thank you, but this is the exact price. Nothing extra is expected."

Ellie took the coins back and bowed a little, which made the man smile. Ivana, watching from a table with her yakisoba, raised her chopsticks in salute. Ellie sat down and turned the practice sheet over, writing a new note to transmit to her future self in Tokyo: pay the exact amount, and do not leave money on the table, because someone will always run after you to give it back.

"Next time I'm ordering dessert too," Ivana said. "In Japanese, if you teach me."

Ellie looked at the dessert case behind the counter and folded the coins into her pocket. "Mochi," she said. "I already know that word."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
Aubrey pushed the coffee table against the wall so the living room had room for two actors and one imaginary dragon. Loukas flopped onto the couch with his script, which was useless, because tonight there was no script. Tomorrow was the drama camp showcase, and Mr. Rao had put them together as a pair for the improv section.

"Remember the rule," Aubrey said, retrieving two hairbrushes from the kitchen drawer to use as microphones. "It's called 'yes, and.' You accept what your partner gives you, and then you add something new."

"I know, I know." Loukas popped up, took a brush, and grinned. "Start."

Aubrey held her brush to her mouth. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival."

"Yes," said Loukas, nodding.

She waited. He kept nodding. The silence stretched until the imaginary crowd probably left. "And?" she finally said.

"And... yes?"

"That's the problem. You keep agreeing but you never add anything, so the scene just stalls, like a car with no gas." She tried again. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival, where a giant pickle has just come to life."

"Yes," said Loukas.

"Add something! Anything! The pickle is doing something."

"Yes... the pickle is standing there."

Aubrey groaned and dropped onto the couch cushion beside him. It was like playing catch with someone who caught the ball and then sat down with it. She stared at the ceiling and thought. Loukas was diligent, honestly. He'd memorized every line of the camp skit in one night. Maybe the problem wasn't effort. Maybe the problem was that he thought agreeing was the whole job, when agreeing was only half.

"Okay, new plan," she said. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you make it weirder. Weirder than my weird. Can you do weird?"

"Excuse me, I am a champion of weird."

"Prove it. Scene: we're two astronauts landing on Mars."

"Yes, and the Mars rover is our tour guide and it only speaks in knock-knock jokes," Loukas said immediately.

Aubrey blinked, then laughed so hard she snorted. "Yes, and the first joke is so bad it knocks over a rock, and the rock rolls downhill and reveals a door."

"Yes, and the door has perfect symmetry, two handles, two windows, and it opens from both sides at once."

"Yes, and behind it is a whole pickle festival, which means we never left Earth!"

They went back and forth for twenty minutes, building a Mars hotel run by a pickle with a clipboard, and the scene never once stalled. When Aubrey's mom leaned in from the kitchen to say it was almost time for Loukas to head home, they both looked up, startled, like they'd actually been on Mars.

"Same time tomorrow before the showcase?" Loukas asked, setting his hairbrush microphone down with great ceremony.

"Yes," said Aubrey, "and bring the dragon."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
story:
Rosalie sat down in the computer lab with the fundraiser notebook open beside the keyboard. Ms. Castillo had given her one job before Friday: turn the class bake sale records into a spreadsheet with a column total and a bar chart, so the principal could see what each table earned. Ameera had already typed the numbers, and now it was Rosalie's turn to make the sheet do the math.

She clicked the empty cell under the column of earnings and typed =SUM(B2:B9). Eight tables, eight numbers. The total appeared: forty-one dollars and fifty cents. Rosalie frowned. She assessed the column again, adding the figures in her head the slow way, table by table. When she got to fifty-five dollars, she stopped. The machine was short by thirteen dollars and fifty cents.

"Can't you just type the right number in?" said Maika, leaning over from the next computer. "The principal won't check."

Rosalie shook her head. "If the total is wrong, the chart is wrong, and then the whole thing is a lie." She looked at the cells one at a time. Seven of them sat snug against the right edge of their boxes, but the number for Table 4, thirteen fifty, huddled on the left side, exactly where words sat. She remembered Ameera pasting that one in from a text message because the Table 4 kids had sent their earnings by phone.

She deleted the cell, typed 13.50 fresh, and pressed Enter. The number jumped to the right edge, and the total at the bottom changed on its own to fifty-five dollars. So that was the rule, she thought, and she felt it click into place like a locker: SUM skipped anything that wasn't a real number, no warning, no red mark. A pasted figure could look like a number and still be nothing but text to the machine, quietly left out.

Then she built the chart. She selected the table names and the earnings, clicked the bar chart button, and the bars rose across the screen. Table 3's bar stood tallest, tall enough to look almost aggressive next to Table 5's stubby little block. She added a title, Class Bake Sale Income, and printed one copy for Ms. Castillo and one for the bulletin board outside the office.

At the door she ran into Ameera, who read the chart upside down and then right side up. "Table 4 did all right," Ameera said. "I thought they'd earned nothing."

"They did earn something," Rosalie said. "The sheet just didn't know it yet." She folded the extra copy and put it in her binder, next to the notebook with all the messy original numbers, the ones she wasn't ready to recycle. Ameera was already walking off down the hall with the good news, and the paper still smelled faintly warm from the printer.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
story:
Piper slapped the crumpled sign on Mr. Rowe's desk before the bell finished ringing. "The bookstore by the mall banned backpacks. That's a violation of my Charter rights. Section 8, unreasonable search."

Mr. Rowe picked up the sign and read it. "Assignment's due Friday, Piper. You have to explain a right in your own words. This is a start."

"Better than a start. It's real." She pointed at the small print: NO BACKPACKS. NO EXCEPTIONS. "They searched Loic's bag last Saturday. Made him open it right at the counter."

After class she found Loic and Terrence at the lockers and laid out her plan. "If the Charter protects us, we test it. We walk in with the backpacks and cite the section. If they back down, the rule doesn't restrict us anymore."

"Or we get banned from the only bookstore we can walk to," Terrence said.

Loic shrugged. "I'm in. I still want my money back anyway."

Saturday, Piper led them through the door with her backpack straps gripped tight. The same clerk stepped in front of the counter. "Read the sign."

"I did. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms says you can't search us without reason."

The clerk folded his arms. "Kid, we're not the government. The Charter applies to governments, not to us."

Piper froze. She had read the whole document twice for the assignment and never once thought about who it was aimed at. The clerk waited, arms still crossed, and she realized he wasn't guessing. "You're sure?"

"My sister's a lawyer. I've heard the speech a hundred times."

They bought nothing and walked out. Terrence kicked a pebble across the parking lot. "So we can't do anything?"

"There's still the assignment," Piper said slowly, pulling out her phone. She searched the Charter's text, scanning for the words that mattered. Governments. The word sat there in her notes from Monday, circled twice, and she had skipped right past it. "Okay. New idea. The sign isn't a Charter problem. But the city bus kicked me off last month for the same reason, and the bus is the government. That's my example."

"You're going to write about yourself?" Loic asked.

"I'm going to write about the difference." She was already typing notes. "Friday, Mr. Rowe's going to ask who did their project on a real event. Mine's going to be the only one with a twist."

Terrence squinted at her. "What twist?"

Piper held up the phone, showing a photo she'd taken of the bookstore's front window. Below the NO BACKPACKS sign sat a smaller plaque: PROPERTY OF THE CITY LIBRARY BOARD.

Loic leaned in. "Is a library board the government?"

Piper grinned and pocketed the phone. "Ask my essay."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
story:
Ethan's fingers hit the last chord of "The Little Peasant Dance" a full eight seconds before the recording ended. He pulled his hands off the community centre piano and stared at the clock on the wall. Mr. González had given every piano student a spot in the Friday recital, but at this rate Ethan would finish his piece while everyone else was still settling into their chairs. Why did he always rush? He didn't feel fast inside. The music felt slow to him, steady even, yet somehow the clock said otherwise.

"You did it again," said Mouhamed, who was sprawled on the bench beside him with his trumpet case open. "Giuliana timed you. Sixty-one seconds. She says the recording is one minute and ten."

"Maybe the recording is wrong," Ethan said, though he doubted it. Giuliana appeared from behind the upright piano in the corner, holding her phone like a piece of evidence.

"The recording is fine. You're impulsive. You play every loud part faster." She tapped her phone. "Watch. You cruised through the middle section where it gets loud."

Ethan played just the middle section while she timed him, then played it again while pretending it was quiet, like a whisper. The quiet version took longer. That was strange. The notes were exactly the same in both versions. Same fingers, same keys, same everything. Somehow the loudness itself was dragging him forward, like a dog pulling a leash. But how could you notice something happening inside your own hands? It was like trying to watch your own eyes blink.

Then he remembered the shelf in the supply room, where Mr. González kept old method books and a strange pyramid-shaped brass box with a sliding weight on a metal arm. Mr. González had called it a metronome once. Ethan fetched it, wound the key, and set the weight the way Mr. González had shown a younger student last month. Tick, tick, tick. The sound was stubborn and even, refusing to hurry no matter what.

"Play with that," Giuliana said. "We'll verify it. You against the machine."

Ethan started the piece, matching his notes to the ticks. Whenever he pulled ahead, the tick landed behind him like a reproach, and he eased back. When the loud middle section arrived, he felt the old tug, but now he had something outside himself to check against, something that couldn't be charmed into speeding up. He finished, breathing hard. Giuliana looked up from her phone. "One minute and nine seconds."

Mouhamed leaned over the brass box. "Who even invented this thing?"

"Mr. González said a guy named Maelzel," Ethan said. "Johann Nepomuk Maelzel. He patented it in 1815."

"Patented? Like an invention?"

"Like an invention." Ethan slid the weight a notch lower, and the ticking slowed to a patient walk. He wondered what it would feel like to master a slow tempo instead of just surviving it. He set his hands on the keys again.

"Count me in," Giuliana said, thumb hovering over the timer. "Ready? Go."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Jessica pushed the folded poster board down the hallway toward Room 12, where the sign-language club met on Thursdays. Fraser had asked her to make the poster because her lettering was the neatest in grade eight, and the club needed members or it would be cancelled. She had lettered WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in big blue capitals, and now she stood in the doorway holding it up.

Fraser's face went strange, half pleased and half worried. "Almost," he said. "Can you change one thing?"

Jessica frowned at her own work. She had spent two evenings on the swan curves of the F's. "Which thing?"

"Deaf has to be capital D." Fraser's hands moved while he talked, because that was how he talked with his cousin, quick shapes like birds taking off. "Lowercase deaf is the hearing condition. Capital D is the community, the culture, the sign language, all of it. James Woodward proposed that in 1972."

"Who's James Woodward?"

"No idea. My cousin told me. He said everybody in the club would know, and some people feel strongly about it."

Jessica sat down at the craft table with her pencil and eraser. She had made an assumption, she realized, that the word was just a word, and she felt vulnerable holding up her mistake in front of the whole room. The laminator smelled like warm plastic, and someone's phone was playing music too quietly to name the song.

She erased the lowercase d and redrew it tall, matching her other capitals. Then she tested the idea on Francois, who was taping the doorway and pretending not to eavesdrop. "If I write Deaf with a capital, does that include you, even though you can hear?"

Francois considered this while smoothing a wrinkle out of the tape. "I think that's the point. I'm learning sign because my grandmother went deaf at forty, small d. But me coming here, that's the big D part."

Jessica looked at the poster again, and a doubt crept in. She turned to Fraser. "So it's not wrong to write deaf lowercase ever?"

"It depends what you mean," Fraser said. "My cousin uses both about himself."
