The adviser, Mr. Wiśniewski, leaned over from the next table where he was fixing the popcorn machine, and Jessica braced for a lecture. He only shrugged and said, "Ask them yourself," and nodded toward the door, where three students she had never met were peering in at the poster.

The tallest one read it slowly, lips moving, then looked at Jessica. "Who made this?"

"I did," she said, holding it a little tighter. "Should I change it back?"

The student smiled, but did not answer right away.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, which meant August had found something in his grandmother's photo box again. This time it was a birthday card his grandfather had sent her in 1994, signed in careful blue ink: "Szabó István." August posted a picture of it with the caption, "My grandpa signed his own name wrong?? On a CARD???" Cade replied with three crying-laughing faces and the words "one job," and then the two of them began composing a corrective reply to a man who had been dead since 2009.

Lillian typed "wait" three times before anyone stopped. She was staring at the signature, and something about it was snagging in her brain the way a sleeve catches on a nail. In her history class, Ms. Yilmaz had put a roster on the board for a unit on family trees, and half the names had looked backwards to Lillian too: Kim Ji-ho, Wang Mei, Tanaka Aiko. Ms. Yilmaz had called roll that day and said the second name first, every time, without stopping to explain. So Lillian went to the class site, pulled up the unit, and found the worksheet she'd half-ignored in September. There it was in the margin, in her own handwriting because Ms. Yilmaz made them copy the tricky bits: In Hungarian, the family name comes before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.

"It's not wrong," she posted. "Hungarian puts the family name first. Same as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Szabó is his last name." The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in group-chat time was roughly a geological era. Then August sent a single "??????" and Cade wrote, "so his name is István Szabó and he wrote it the Hungarian way? on purpose?" Lillian confirmed it, and August replied that he had spent nine years of his life calling his grandfather "Grandpa Szabó" at family dinners while apparently using the correct order entirely by accident.

The next message was a photo of another card, this one from 2001, signed "Kovács Erzsébet," which August had always assumed was some aunt he'd never met. "That's my grandma," he wrote. "She's alive. I'm texting her." Ten minutes later he reported back: she had replied with a paragraph about the village where she grew up, where a peasant farmer on her street had been the only person with a telephone, and where she had nurtured a habit of signing her name properly because her schoolteacher had rapped knuckles over anything less. She closed, August said, by hoping he wasn't becoming one of those people who found handwriting obsolete, since a typed name told you nothing about a person.

Cade asked whether this meant he'd been filing Japanese names backwards in his head all through elementary school, and Lillian said basically yes. August changed the group chat name to "Szabó István Memorial Correct Order Society" and pinned the photo of the card to the top. Then he posted one more picture: his grandmother's reply, ending with the line, "Tell your friends the phone is not always right, but grandmothers usually are."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
The dinner reservation was for six o'clock sharp, and the movie started at eight, which left Maelie exactly one hour and forty minutes to eat, apologize for nothing, and figure out why Zakary's grandmother kept looking at her like she had spilled something.

She hadn't spilled anything. She had checked.

It was Zakary's birthday, and his whole family had taken over the big round table at the restaurant near the mall. When Maelie arrived, the grandmother had pressed a small red envelope into her hands, and Maelie, who had brought a wrapped sketchbook for Zakary, had stood there holding both like she couldn't do math. She'd said thank you twice, then a third time, which made the grandmother smile, at least.

The trouble started with the ribs. They were glazed and slippery, and Maelie needed both hands, so she planted her chopsticks upright in her rice bowl the way she would have parked a pencil in a cup, reached over, and grabbed the biggest piece.

The grandmother's smile dwindle. Zakary's mother stopped pouring tea mid-stream. Across the table, Zakary made a small strangled noise.

"Maelie," he said quietly. "Take them out of the rice."

"Why?" Maelie looked down. Her chopsticks stood straight up out of the white rice like two little poles. They weren't hurting anything. "They'll roll off if I lay them down."

"Just take them out. Please. I'll explain later."

"Explain now. We have a movie at eight and I am not eating this entire dinner in the dark."

Zakary leaned across the birthday cake that hadn't even been lit yet. "Standing up in rice, chopsticks look like incense for the dead," he said, wincing. "So nobody leaves them like that. Rest them on the bowl edge. Or the holder. Like this." He laid his own pair across the top of his bowl.

Maelie pulled hers out fast, and the grandmother exhaled and went back to her tea. Maelie set her chopsticks down carefully, then picked them up again, then set them down again, testing the angle like the whole table was wired with voltage and one wrong move would light her up.

"Okay," she said. "New theory. Everything I do at this table is being graded."

"Nobody's grading you," Zakary said. "You got the envelope right. You used both hands. That was good."

She thought back. Both hands, yes. She'd done that without knowing why, just copying his mother. So there were rules, and the rules had reasons, and the reasons weren't written anywhere she could read them. She decided to run a test before the cake came: she refilled the grandmother's teacup, with both hands, and waited.

The grandmother said something to Zakary's mother, and they both laughed, and the grandmother patted Maelie's wrist.

"What did she say?" Maelie whispered.

"She said you learn faster than Zakary did, and that he once stuck his chopsticks in the rice at his own birthday dinner."

"I did not," Zakary said. "I was seven. That's not evidence."

Maelie checked the clock above the kitchen door. Six forty-two. Cake, then presents, then the movie, and she still had two pieces of rib to finish. She picked up her chopsticks properly this time, snapped up the biggest one, and held it out toward Zakary.

"Happy birthday," she said. "You almost died at seven. That's the best gift I've heard all night."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
Jackson's family reunion was supposed to mean the whole afternoon at the lake, and the first thing he heard when he got out of the car was his little cousin refusing to go near the water. "Sharks," the boy said, arms crossed on the dock. "I saw a video about a boy who got bitten."

"There aren't sharks in this lake," Jackson said.

"There could be." The boy sat down on the boards and announced that he would not swim, not even to cool off, and the adults were already starting a negotiation over popsicles to get him to at least put his feet in. Jackson gave up and went to find Sofia and Billy, who had come with their families to the same gathering.

"The shark video had millions of views," Billy said when Jackson told them. "It was all over everything this summer. That one kid." He scrolled through his phone and held it up. A boy in a hospital bed, holding up a bandaged arm, grinning at the camera.

"It's weird," Sofia said. "My mom showed me the same story, and now my little brother won't get in our pool. A pool. And nothing ever happened to anyone we actually know."

Jackson turned his popsicle stick over in his fingers. One video, one kid, and now two little boys wouldn't swim. He thought about his science unit, where Ms. Flores had made them compare a tested claim to a single report. A tested claim held up across lots of cases. A single report was just one person's experience, vivid as anything, and it told you almost nothing about how often a thing happened. One story could feel like proof even when it wasn't. "So the question isn't whether it happened," he said. "It's how many times it happened out of all the times it could have."

They needed numbers, so they asked for phones and counted. Billy found the count of shark bites on swimmers for the whole coast last year: a few dozen, in a country where tens of millions of people go in the ocean. Then they counted the crowd at the reunion itself, about forty people, and figured that if every single one of them swam in the ocean every summer for the rest of their lives, the odds that any of them would ever be bitten stayed vanishingly small. Sofia wrote the numbers on a paper plate with a marker.

Jackson brought the plate to the dock and sat down next to his cousin. "You know the video was real," he said. "But real and common aren't the same thing. Here's how many bites there were, and here's how many people swam. It's like being scared of vending machines because one guy got hurt by one." He tapped the plate. "You remember the shark kid because the video was everywhere. You don't remember the millions of boring swims, because nobody films those."

"There's a name for that," Sofia said, coming up behind them with Billy. "Tversky and Kahneman called it the availability heuristic. In 1973. You judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind."

The boy looked at the numbers on the plate for a while, then at the lake, flat and glittering with nothing under it but weeds and one lost flip-flop from last summer. "Sharks still scare me," he said.

"Fine. Be scared and swim anyway," Jackson said. "I'll hold your hand until it ceases to matter, and then we race."

The boy stood up, tested the water with one toe, and jumped in with a splash that soaked the paper plate, numbers and all.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic, and Jacob held the box with both hands while the cashier rang it up. His mom had said the phone was his, and his alone, which meant the mistakes would be his alone too. Kye and Jax had come along, and they crowded around as Jacob peeled off the shrink wrap right there at the counter.

"First app," Kye said. "Get a flashlight."

Jacob searched for it and tapped install. A box popped up on the screen. The flashlight app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all his contacts. He stared at it.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Jax asked. "It's a light."

Jacob thought about it. A flashlight did one job, and that job did not involve calling anyone. He could not see why the app wanted those things, and he did not like not being able to see why. He imagined everyone in his contacts list, all his aunts and his teachers and Mr. Berg from next door, being handed over to some app for no reason. He tapped deny, deny, deny, and installed it anyway. The flashlight worked fine.

Later that week, he was still thinking about it. If an app had to ask before it could use the camera, microphone, or contacts, then somewhere in the phone there had to be a record of what he had said yes to. He went into settings and dug around until he found a list of every app and what it was allowed to do. There it was. He scrolled through and diagnosed the problem right away: a weather app he had installed on Tuesday had permission to use his microphone, and he had agreed without reading. He tapped the little switch next to microphone and turned it off. He checked the camera and contacts too, and switched those off wherever an app had them but did not seem to need them.

At school on Monday, Kye brought it up again. "You were so paranoid at the store," he said.

"It asked for my contacts," Jacob said. "A flashlight."

"So what did you do?"

"Denied it. And I can take it back later in settings, if I ever say yes by accident."

Jax pulled out his own phone, found his app list, and went quiet. His flashlight app had contacts, camera, and microphone all switched on. He turned them off one by one, and his ears went red, but nobody said anything about the humiliation of it, because Kye was too busy checking his own phone.

At home, Jacob's mom asked how the phone was going. He said it was fine, and that he was keeping the settings screen handy. Then he took the phone out, opened the flashlight, and shined it at the ceiling.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
Cooper spread the newspaper clipping across the library table and read it aloud to Adelie and Leela. "'The new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste.'" He tapped the page. "This guy says our park is a waste."

"My dad says people write letters like that when they don't skate," Adelie said, dropping her backpack onto a chair.

Cooper pulled out his debate notebook. He had signed up to argue at the next city council meeting, and Ms. Girma had told him the library kept the meeting minutes in the reference section. His argument needed to be solid, not just loud. "If I'm going to answer this letter, I have to know which parts of it I can actually refute."

"Refute how?" Leela asked, flipping the clipping toward herself.

"Like, prove wrong. But look." Cooper drew a line down the middle of a fresh page. On the left he wrote "two million dollars" and underlined it. "That's either true or it isn't. Somebody can look it up. The city budget would show it." On the right side he wrote "a waste" and stared at it. "But that part, I can't look that up anywhere. There's no budget line for waste."

Adelie leaned over the notebook. "So one sentence, but two different kinds of thing in it?"

"Right." Cooper stood and went to the reference shelf. The minutes from last spring were bound in blue folders, and he found the vote on the skate park without much trouble. There it was: the contractor's bid, two million dollars, approved six to one. He carried the folder back to the table. "The number checks out. So the letter writer got the cost right, and I can't refute that part no matter how much I want to."

Leela frowned at the clipping. "Then what do you argue?"

Cooper copied the bid number into his notebook, then the vote count, then the date the park opened. He wrote slowly, because he was thinking. "The 'a waste' part. That's just his opinion. It can't be checked. But the number of people who use the park, that can." He looked up. "If I count skaters on a Saturday, that's a checkable number. My whole Saturday, gone, but it's a real count."

"Then his 'waste' claim has to stand against actual numbers," Adelie said.

"Exactly. And here's the weird part." Cooper tapped the original sentence again. "One sentence can mix both. The cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion. Same sentence." He grinned and closed the folder. "Leela, you're good at counting. I'll need a tally sheet."

"Bring two pencils," she said. "And my board."

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Paint can often be partly lifted from watercolour paper by dabbing the area with a damp brush or clean tissue, which softens an edge or lightens a spot.
story:
Vincent had been diligent about his watercolour portrait for exactly three days, and today the cheeks were going to ruin everything. He had mixed what he thought was a soft rose for the blush on his subject's face, but the wash had gone on dark as a strawberry, and it was drying fast.

"It looks like she ran a marathon," said Keenan, leaning over from the next easel in Ms. Lindqvist's art room. "In the desert."

"Thanks. Very helpful." Vincent stared at the paper. Ms. Lindqvist had drilled one rule into them all week: build the portrait light to dark, layer by layer, because watercolour was unforgiving. He'd assumed unforgiving meant permanent, which meant the portrait was finished before it started.

Inaaya appeared behind him with her damp brush in hand. "Hold on. Watch this." She touched a clean tissue to the too-dark cheek and pressed lightly, then again with a corner of the tissue. When she lifted it away, the blush was lighter, the edge softer, and the strawberry had turned into something closer to a real blush.

"Wait. You can extract the paint? After it's on?" Vincent grabbed his own brush, wet it, and dabbed it against his subject's other cheek, then pressed tissue to the spot. Paint came up into the tissue, leaving the paper paler. He laughed out loud, and the kid across the room looked over to see what was so exciting.

"It's not a miracle," Inaaya said. "Ms. Lindqvist mentioned it Monday. You were probably staring at your palette."

He had been staring at his palette, actually. He'd spent the whole week treating watercolour like a treaty he couldn't break, one wrong move and the deal was off, portrait over. Now he was renegotiating. He dabbed again along the jaw where the shadow had gone too heavy, testing how much pressure lifted how much colour, how far he could push it before the paper started to fuzz.

"We should sign something," Keenan said, holding up his own ruined background, a sky gone stormy grey when he'd wanted pale morning. "A formal treaty. You teach me the dabbing trick, I give you my last chocolate milk at lunch."

"Done," Vincent said, and shook on it, already wetting his brush for Keenan's sky.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
story:
The bus to Camp Wanasetta smelled like sunscreen and somebody's granola bars, and Livia sat with her duffel between her knees like a guard dog. She had wanted to come, that was the thing. She had begged for two weeks in a lake cabin while her friends stayed home, and now that the trees were sliding past the window, she wished she had begged a little less.

Her cabin had four girls, and by the second night Livia had an alliance with Layan, who could braid hair, and a wary truce with Colt, who could burp the alphabet. Their counselor was Ms. Dela Cruz, who ran the waterfront and laughed loud at her own jokes. On Wednesday they earned a campfire: hot dogs, burnt marshmallows, a song about a moose that Colt ruined on purpose. When the fire burned down to gray coals, the girls started walking back to the cabin, and Livia followed for three steps before something snagged in her mind. The night before, she had watched Ms. Dela Cruz stand over the fire ring long after everyone else left, stirring the ash with a stick like she was looking for something.

"Wait," Livia said. "I don't think it's out."

Layan squinted at the ring. "It looks out. There's not even smoke."

"Smoke isn't the part you can see that matters," Livia said, though she wasn't sure that made sense until she said it. She ran back to the ring, grabbed the water bucket, and poured. The ash hissed and a curl of steam rose, and underneath, deep in the pile, an orange eye blinked open. She stabbed at it with the stirring stick until the orange closed, poured water again, and the whole ring went dark and quiet.

Ms. Dela Cruz came through the trees with her flashlight swinging. "What did I tell you all this afternoon?" she said, half scolding, half smiling.

"You said it at lunch," Layan said. "Drown it, stir it, drown it again. Then feel for heat, because if a fire is too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

"Too hot to touch is too hot to leave," Livia repeated, and held her palm above the ash, then lower, then touching. Warm, but not burning. She kept her hand there longer than she needed to, feeling the small heat that had been hiding under all that innocent gray.

Ms. Dela Cruz let them stay up past lights-out as a reward, and they sat on the cabin steps while Colt named constellations she made up on the spot. Livia should have been happy, and she was, mostly. But lying in her bunk later, listening to Layan breathe, she thought about how she had spent the whole first day homesick, writing a letter she never mailed, and how the only reason she knew to check that fire was because she'd been too miserable to sleep and had watched from her bunk window. The thing that worked for her had come out of the thing that had been worst. Her mom would call that a lesson. Livia just called it strange, and pulled the sleeping bag up to her chin. Outside, somewhere, an owl called twice and went quiet.

At breakfast, Layan slid her the last pancake and said, "You check the fire tonight, okay?"

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Alex had saved thirty-two dollars in a cracked envelope under his mattress, and by Saturday he meant to own a used copy of Iron Hollow, the game everyone at school argued about at lunch. The problem was the online marketplace. Three weeks ago, eleven used copies sat on the listings page at fifteen dollars each. Last night there were only two, and the cheapest one was twenty-six dollars.

"They can't just change the price," Alex said on the bus, holding his phone so Heidi could see the screen. "It's the same disc."

Heidi leaned in. "There's still two left, though. Maybe the price drops again if nobody buys them."

Alex stared at the little green number under each listing. It had never occurred to him that a price could move around like a living thing, pushed by something he couldn't see. He decided to run a test. He would check the page every morning and evening, write down the price and the number of copies, and see whether there was a rule underneath it all.

On Tuesday there were two copies at twenty-six dollars. On Wednesday evening, one copy at twenty-eight. On Thursday morning, still one copy, and a seller named Iron Hollow had dropped it to nineteen dollars. By Thursday night it was gone, sold, and a new listing appeared at fourteen dollars, along with four more used copies in the same genre, all cheap. Alex wrote the numbers in his notebook until his hand ached. When the copies were scarce, the price climbed. When a stack of them showed up, the price sank like a stone in a pond.

He showed the notebook to Reet at lunch. Reet frowned at the columns. "So when lots of people want the scarce ones, the sellers can charge more, and then everybody stops buying?"

"And when the price drops, people buy more again," Alex said. "Heidi calls it the law of demand. It works as long as nothing else changes, like a new sequel coming out."

Reet tapped the page. "You have eighteen dollars and the price is fourteen. That's your window."

That night Alex asked his dad for the laptop, and his pulse did a strange leap when he opened the marketplace. There were six copies now, six, and the cheapest was twelve dollars. He clicked it so fast the touchpad squeaked. He typed his shipping address, checked the box, and pressed Buy.

The confirmation banner glowed at the top of the screen. Alex sat back, and a grin spread across his face, wide and involuntary. From the kitchen his dad called, "Is everything all right in there?"

"Everything is great," Alex shouted. He photographed the screen with his phone to send to Heidi and Reet. "It's coming by Saturday."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A Python for loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without reaching break, which fits 'no divisor found, so the number is prime'.
story:
Eva had promised the whole coding cabin that by Friday demo night her program would ask for a number and say whether it was prime, and right now it said that 9 was prime, which it was not. She sat at the long pine table with her laptop open, running the loop again and watching the wrong answer blink at her. Kash leaned over from the next seat, grinning. "Nine is prime now? You've discovered new math."

"Don't humiliate me before I've had breakfast," Eva said, but her ears went hot anyway. Hana pulled her chair around so she could see the screen.

The problem was the flag. Eva had set a variable called found to zero, and inside the loop she changed it when a divisor appeared, and after the loop she checked it, except the check kept happening too early, or the flag kept its old value from the run before, or something she couldn't see. That was the worst part. The loop did its work somewhere she couldn't look, and the mistake was hiding in there like a bird in a hedge.

"Birds," Hana said suddenly, pointing at the poster taped to the cabin wall, a map dotted with arrows. "Migratory routes. That one crosses the equator twice, look, it goes all the way down and back." Eva looked, mostly to rest her eyes, and thought about how the map showed where the birds went but not why they knew to go there. Her program was like that too. It showed the answer but not the reason underneath.

Then Mr. Chowdhury, the mentor who ran the cabin, came by with his coffee. He read her screen for a moment, took the marker, and wrote four lines on the little whiteboard beside the table. Her loop, but with the word else tucked under it, and her print statement moved inside that block. He tapped the marker once against the board. "Else," he said, and went to refill his coffee, because he never explained anything twice or even once if he could help it.

Eva stared at it. "A loop gets an else?" she said. Hana frowned. Kash shook his head slowly, which meant he didn't know either, which meant nobody at the table knew, which made Eva feel a little better and a lot more curious.

She traced it with her finger on the screen. The else sat under the for, the way an else sits under an if, and the print was inside it. "So if the loop breaks, the else gets skipped," she said, "and if it never breaks, if it checks every number and finds nothing, then the else runs." No divisor found, so the number is prime. She deleted the flag, typed the else, and hit run.

9: not prime. 7: prime. 11: prime. 25: not prime.

"Run it on a million," Kash said. Eva typed it in.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven, but most Protestant churches reject the idea.
story:
The assignment was Adam's idea, which meant it was his job to coordinate it: Yara would handle the interviews, Thalia would bring her grandmother's prayer book, and Adam would find a place to start. He chose the old cemetery behind St. Brigid's, where the stones went back over a hundred years and the caretaker, Mr. Campbell-Brown, let students in after school as long as they closed the gate.

"Grandma's stone is this way," Thalia said, leading them past a row of leaning markers. She stopped at a granite slab with a small crucifix carved at the top, a figure on the cross with her head bowed. Yara found her own family a few rows over, at a plain cross with nothing on it, just clean lines. Adam wrote both descriptions in his notebook and stood between the two graves, tapping his pencil.

"Okay, so here's my theory," he said. "The crucifixes mark the Catholic graves and the plain crosses mark the Protestant ones. If the symbols are different, maybe the teachings are different too. So, Thalia, what does your church say happens after you die?"

Thalia brushed lichen off the edge of her grandmother's stone while she thought. "We go to heaven, but first most people go to purgatory," she said. "It's a purification. Like being cleaned up before you go in."

Yara frowned at her. "My church never says that. We go straight to heaven if we're saved. Pastor Ruiz says purgatory isn't in the Bible at all." The two of them stared at each other, and Adam could almost see the surprise traveling between them, because they had sat three seats apart in homeroom since fifth grade and never once guessed their churches disagreed on something this big.

Mr. Campbell-Brown came around the corner with a spray bottle and a stiff brush, working on a marker crusted with green. "Careful where you stand," he said. "This cleaner's corrosive. It'll eat through your shoe laces faster than the moss." Adam stepped back and asked him about the symbols, and the caretaker nodded slowly. "Catholics put up the crucifix, mostly, and the others keep it plain. Been that way longer than me."

Adam flipped to a fresh page and drew two columns, one headed with a crucifix and one with a plain cross. Under the first he wrote purification first, then heaven, and under the second, straight to heaven, no middle state. Then he added a third line at the bottom, for the question he would ask in class on Monday: what else do the two churches see differently that nobody has told us about? Yara borrowed his pencil to underline it, and Thalia zipped her grandmother's prayer book back into her bag as the shadows of the stones stretched long across the grass.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: One personal story, called anecdotal evidence, cannot prove a general trend, because a single case may not be typical.
story:
Emile pushed the folding table across the gym floor until it screeched against the volleyball line, and Emilien dumped a shoebox of notecards beside him. "This is our case," Emilien said. "Unbeatable." Ms. Henry had taped a sign to the bleachers that read CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT, and under it, in smaller letters, if you can't say the warrant, you don't have a point. Emile picked up the first card. It said, in Emilien's sprawling handwriting, "Cousin Jules failed math because of video games."

"Where's the evidence?" Emile asked. Emilien tapped the card. "It's right there. It happened. I watched it happen." Emile thought back to September, when his mother had blamed a broken dishwasher on the new detergent, and his father had quietly run it twice more with the old detergent before saying a word. It had still been broken. One try had proved nothing either way, his father said later, over the last clean plates they owned. Emile hadn't understood why that mattered until now.

He flipped through the rest of the shoebox. Every card circled back to Cousin Jules. "Your whole case," he said slowly, "is one guy." Emilien frowned. "One guy with a dramatic story." From the free-throw line, Maurice called over that his uncle had eaten video games for breakfast, basically, and done calculus in his sleep. Emilien shouted back that Maurice's uncle didn't count because he was "a statistical monster," which was somehow the funniest thing anyone had said all week, and even Ms. Henry, shelving the pinnies, put a hand over her mouth.

Emile laid the cards out in rows, like a coach drawing a play. "Look. Claim: games hurt grades. Evidence: Jules. That's it. There's no warrant connecting one cousin to every student in the school." He picked up a fresh card. "We need to quantify it. Survey thirty kids, games and grades, count them." "Counting is boring," Emilien said. "Counting wins," Emile said. "Ms. Henry's whole system is about being systematic. Claim, evidence, warrant, every single point, no skipping." He glanced up at the sign on the bleachers. "And there's a word for your cousin thing. Anecdotal evidence." Emilien squinted. "Is that an insult?" "It's a category," Emile said. "The category of stories that prove nothing."

Emilien looked at his shoebox, then at Jules's card, then at the empty gym, where thirty desks' worth of students would show up for the debate on Friday. He groaned the groan of a boy about to do real work, and Maurice jogged over with a clipboard he had clearly stolen from the equipment room. "Survey?" Maurice said. "I'll do the hallway before lunch. That's my zone." Emile handed him a pencil. "Fifteen before, fifteen after," he said. "And Jules?" Emilien held up the card, studied it one last time, then clipped it to the bottom of the stack, face down. "Backup material," he said. "For the emotional finale."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
The message landed at 4:32 on a Tuesday, right when Christopher was supposed to be meeting Joey and Kurt at the basketball courts behind the school. He pulled out his phone under the bleachers and saw it glowing at the top of the group chat: WHERE ARE YOU, in letters so big and black they seemed to jump off the screen. It was from Kurt. Below it, Joey had already replied, "why are you yelling? lol."

Christopher typed back "omw 5 min" and started jogging. On the way he scrolled up through the chat, because something felt off. Kurt never wrote in capitals. His usual messages were all lowercase, drifting and lazy, things like "maybe i'll come" and "idk might be tired." Today there were three caps messages in a row. WHERE ARE YOU. THEN FORGET IT. NOT WAITING HERE ALL DAY.

At the courts, Kurt was sitting on the far bench with his hood up, spinning a ball on one finger. He didn't look up when Christopher jogged through the gate. Joey was shooting free throws, and he mouthed "good luck" with a grin that said he was planning to enjoy this.

"Hey," Christopher said. "Got held up in science. Mr. Iyer kept us late because half the class turned in, like, one paragraph."

"Whatever," Kurt said, still spinning the ball.

Christopher sat down on the bench. He had a theory forming, and he tested it the way he tested things, carefully, out loud. "You wrote in all caps today. Joey thought you were yelling at us."

"I was not yelling," Kurt said, finally looking up. "It's just typing."

"Kind of yelling, though," Joey called from the foul line. The ball clanked off the rim. "Everybody reads caps that way. It's like shouting on a screen."

Kurt frowned at his phone like it had betrayed him. "Nobody answers my normal messages," he said. "I type 'anyone at the courts' and it just sits there for an hour. I type it big and you two show up in five minutes."

Christopher checked the chat history to be sure, scrolling back two weeks. He counted. Kurt's lowercase messages got answered, on average, maybe once in five, a rough ratio of one reply for every five sent. Then again, half of those had been sent at ten at night, when everyone else's phones were off, so quiet hours and being ignored often coincided. The caps messages had been sent at peak time, right after school. That was probably the whole difference. "It's not the size," Christopher said. "It's the timing. You text us at ten p.m. and expect us to answer. Nobody's awake. My phone is off and I'm lethargic by then anyway, half asleep on the couch."

"So I shouted for nothing," Kurt said.

"You shouted and it worked out badly," Joey said, jogging over. "Christopher showed up because you texted at the right time, and now we all think you're mad."

Kurt pulled his hood down. There was a silence that was almost funny, the three of them standing there while the truth sat in the middle of the court like a loose ball nobody wanted to pick up. "I wasn't mad," Kurt said. "I just wanted to play."

"Then next time type like a normal person," Christopher said, "with one or two question marks, and maybe wait longer than nine minutes before declaring an emergency."

"Nine minutes," Joey repeated, delighted. "It was nine minutes."

"Fine, fine." Kurt stood up, bounced the ball once, hard. "First to eleven. Losers explain group chat etiquette to Mr. Iyer."

"He already knows," Christopher said, taking position at the top of the key. "He's the only one who types in lowercase and still gets answers."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
Romy had six minutes to figure out how the new student should be greeted, and her spreadsheet of welcome ideas had failed her completely. She sat in the empty computer lab, scrolling through a school database of international student records that Ms. Joshi had left open on the desktop. Faris, transferring from a school in New Zealand, was arriving today, and Romy, as head of the welcome committee, wanted the greeting to be right. Not an approximate guess, but right.

She had one clue. In the notes column of his file, a previous teacher had written a single strange line: "greets with hongi." Romy searched the word and found a photo of two people pressing their noses and foreheads together, eyes almost closed. She read that it was a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand, and that it meant the sharing of the breath of life. She read it twice, because it sounded made up, like something Kabir would invent for a bet.

She decided to test it. If she offered her hand and Faris expected a hongi, the moment would go stiff and wrong, and a whole year of awkward homeroom mornings would be thwarted before it began. So at the door of the gym, when Faris arrived with his aunt and a box of mangoes for the class, Romy leaned in and pressed her nose and forehead gently against his. For a second he was completely still. Then he smiled so wide that his aunt laughed, and Kabir, holding the banner behind them, nearly dropped it.

"You know the hongi," Faris said.

"It's for sharing the breath of life," Romy said. "Right?"

He nodded and handed her a mango, and she gave him the welcome folder she had decorated, because in her grandmother's house no guest ever arrived without a gift and no host ever let one leave without one. Faris turned the folder over in his hands like it was something rare. In return his aunt insisted Romy keep a mango, refusing three times before Romy understood that refusing back was part of the game.

At lunch, Faris sat with his elbows off the table, waiting until everyone was served before he ate, while Kabir tore his parantha with his fingers and reached across for the pickle. Romy watched them both and realized politeness was not one rule but a hundred different ones, and the only way to learn them was to lean in, nose first.

"Same time tomorrow?" Faris asked, lifting his mango.

"Same time tomorrow," Romy said, and pressed her palm flat on the table like a promise.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
story:
Victor had the folded paper in his back pocket all through school, and the moment he got home he spread it on the kitchen table like a treasure map. His prescription, the optometrist had called it, and next to two sets of numbers were the letters OD and OS. He'd assumed OD meant something ordinary until Winnie, peering over his shoulder on the bus, had gone quiet and said, "Sinister is right there. OS. That can't be good." Now Victor sat alone at the table, turning the paper toward the window light, trying to decide whether to be worried.

He texted Winnie, who lived two houses down, and she arrived within minutes with her bike helmet still on. "Did you look it up?" she asked.

"No. I want to figure it out first." He tapped the paper. "There's a trick my grandpa, a veteran, uses for puzzles. Read what's actually there, not what you're afraid of. The doctor measured my eyes one at a time, remember? She covered my left eye, then my right. So the two lines have to mean one eye each." He covered his own left eye with his palm and squinted at the clock across the kitchen. The numbers were a smear. Then he covered his right eye, and the clock sharpened a little, still fuzzy but readable. "My right eye is the worse one. Now I just need to know which line is the right eye."

"That's the scary line," Winnie said. "The one with more numbers."

Victor studied the paper. The OD line had the bigger numbers. If his right eye was worse, and OD held the bigger correction, then OD had to be his right eye, and OS his left. "It fits," he said slowly. "But I don't know why they'd call it that."

He called the optometrist's office. The receptionist put him on hold, and a second voice came on, an older woman who sounded like she'd answered this question a thousand times. "OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister," she said. "It's on every prescription we write."

Winnie let out a breath. "So sinister just means left. I donated a whole afternoon to being scared of that."

"You were scared for both of us," Victor said, and she laughed. He thanked the woman and hung up, then carried the paper to the fridge and pinned it under the magnet shaped like a slice of pizza. In a week the actual glasses would arrive, and the clock on the wall, the one that had been a smear for months, would have crisp black hands and readable numbers.

"Come on," Winnie said, grabbing his sleeve. "Before your mom gets home, let's test your bad eye on the stop sign at the corner. I'll cover one at a time."
